items.title: iOS 27 is now available with big changes to Photos, and Siri
items.summary: Apple has released iOS 27 to the public, bringing with it the long-awaited overhaul of Siri among other AI-based changes to your iPhone.
items.content_html:
Apple has released iOS 27 to the public, bringing with it the long-awaited overhaul of Siri among other AI-based changes to your iPhone.

Introduced back in June at WWDC 2026, Apple's update to iOS 27 has undergone many developer beta and public beta passes. But now, with the release of the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max on the horizon, it's made it available to all iPhone users.

Apple is continuing with its current numbering strategy of referring to the year that the operating system will be used the most in. That would be a small part of 2026 but nine months of 2027.

As usual, users can expect some changes from the operating system update. One of them is a very long-awaited change.

iOS 27: Siri AI and Apple Intelligence

The big news this time is that Apple has finally implemented its Siri overhaul. The change announced during WWDC 2024 and delayed in early 2025 has become a reality.

Using the Apple Foundation Model trained by Google Gemini, Siri in iOS 27 is being supercharged, as is all of Apple Intelligence in general.

As well as the new model, there's now a System Orchestrator that combines all of the elements that make up Apple Intelligence into a cohesive whole.

That means you're tapping the same systems if you're dealing with images, text, or anything else.

Siri AI now uses contextual awareness and your data more. Image Credit: Apple

The primary way that everyone will experience this will be through Siri, now dubbed Siri AI. With a new Liquid Glass appearance that consumes the Dynamic Island, it works much like old Siri with verbal prompts, but there's also text entry and a new Siri AI app.

The app is your destination for checking over previous conversations you've had with Siri. Those discussions are also more conversational, with follow-up questions and prompts.

It brings Siri and Apple Intelligence more in line with other AI chatbot services. However, the new contextual awareness will make it seem more impressive.

Siri can now take advantage of your data, your contacts, and messaging history, in answering queries. For example, if you ask where you went on your last vacation, Siri could bring up shots from your trip, referencing comments in your messages planning the event, and tourist spots you passed through.

However, while any device with Apple Intelligence support can use Siri AI, only some will benefit from using Apple's new "most advanced on-device model ever." That means the iPhone Air and iPhone 17 Pro and later will be able to use those new LLMs.

iOS 27: Images and Photos

The changes aren't just about Siri, but they also apply to other areas.

For example, Visual Intelligence is now much easier to access in the Camera app thanks to a new Siri mode. Taking a shot, you can then use what's visible in the image as part of a Siri query.

You're not limited to the camera either. You can even take a screenshot and make a Siri query from that.

Siri mode in the Camera app

In the Photos app, there are now new editing options driven by AI. That includes Extend, which can generate more of an image for you beyond what the camera saw.

There's also Spatial Reframe, which lets you change the camera angle after you took the shot. It's advised not to push it too far, though.

Spatial reframing of a portrait of a kitten works well. Original on the left.

Image Playground, Apple's image generation feature, has been enhanced since iOS 26 with ChatGPT integration. That means being able to create images in more styles, including photorealistic graphics.

iOS 27: Child Safety

Parental controls have been a continual area of complaint from groups concerned about the safety of their children. Once again, Apple is trying to appease them with a new set of features.

The parental controls have been revamped in iOS 27, including making it a lot easier for a parent to set up a new child Apple Account. Parents will also be guided on how to modify a child's access to apps on a device.

While children could ask for access to an app before, the iOS 27 update expands these requests to include websites.

The Time Allowances feature of Screen Time now makes it easier to manage app usage. APIs also allow developers to hook into that system.

There's also an update to Communication Safety. Before, it would block nudity from view, but now it will also hide gore.

iOS 27: Smaller changes

These are the main things to look out for in iOS 27, but there are many other much smaller changes too.

The controversial Liquid Glass aesthetic has been given some tweaks to make it more readable. Better contrast, sharper icons, and a customization slider are available in this release.

On the health side, GymKit on iPhone now means you can connect it to compatible cardio equipment at a gym. If you have AirPods Pro 3, you can also use it to track your heart rate with those workouts.

Perimenopause and Menopause support in Health's Cycle Tracking will now notify users if logged cycle patterns are suggestive of perimenopause.

Old Apple Maps and new iOS 27 Apple Maps. Note the changes in how the trees are rendered.

Apple Maps now has better Flyover imagery, enhanced with Visual Intelligence. Local Lists will automate lists of restaurants and other topics based on the interactions of other users.

There are also enhancements to the Home app with Apple Intelligence. Notifications can be combined, HomeKit Secure Video footage can be described to you before you watch it, and AI can now help you search for specific clips.

HomeKit Secure Video also now streams and records in 4K.

iOS 27: Compatibility and Installation

IOS 27 will be compatible with the iPhone 11 and later models, as well as the second-generation iPhone SE and later. This is the same compatibility list as iOS 26, meaning no models have been dropped off the roster.

The full list of compatible models that can update to iOS 27 follows.

  • iPhone 17 Pro
  • iPhone 17 Pro Max
  • iPhone 16e
  • iPhone 16
  • iPhone 16 Plus
  • iPhone 16 Pro
  • iPhone 16 Pro Max
  • iPhone 15
  • iPhone 15 Plus
  • iPhone 15 Pro
  • iPhone 15 Pro Max
  • iPhone 14
  • iPhone 14 Plus
  • iPhone 14 Pro
  • iPhone 14 Pro Max
  • iPhone 13
  • iPhone 13 mini
  • iPhone 13 Pro
  • iPhone 13 Pro Max
  • iPhone 12
  • iPhone 12 mini
  • iPhone 12 Pro
  • iPhone 12 Pro Max
  • iPhone 11
  • iPhone 11 Pro
  • iPhone 11 Pro Max
  • iPhone SE (2nd generation or later)

To install iOS 27 onto an iPhone, open the Settings app, tap General, then Software Update. Tap the iOS 27 update and follow the instructions.

For participants in the developer and public beta programs, the update may appear automatically with the final version. In some cases, you may have to tap Beta Updates and set it to Off.

New owners of the iPhone 18 Pro will not need to install the update, as it will be preinstalled on their hardware.

items.title: macOS Golden Gate is here and Siri AI is its remarkable best
items.summary: After months of beta testing, Apple has released macOS Golden Gate. As always, it's a mix, but there are great improvements and Siri AI is mostly fantastic.
items.content_html:
After months of beta testing, Apple has released macOS Golden Gate. As always, it's a mix, but there are great improvements and Siri AI is mostly fantastic.

Fantastic is a strong word but apart from a few aspects that are still startlingly poor in it, Siri AI deserves the description. Up to now, Siri has really been an iPhone tool as it was cumbersome and slow on the Mac, and simply not as useful there.

Going straight into Siri AI

Now, incorporated into Spotlight so that it is always a keystroke within reach, Siri AI transforms the macOS Siri experience entirely. Gone is the tiny popup in a corner, and what's most welcome is that the need to stop typing and wait for Siri's response is gone too.

With macOS Golden Gate, you can call up Spotlight, ask Siri AI to find that email where you told that charity some dimensions for an advert some time, and carry on working. Faster than you could ever find that three-year-old email, Siri AI is back with exactly the answer.

But truly, the fact that you can carry on working while it looks is as transformative as what it is now capable of doing. The Spotlight/Siri AI black dialog box does pop up in the middle of your screen, but you can drag it out of the way and carry on typing in your document.

I now use Siri AI whenever I want something that I know is on my Mac somewhere, whether that's a document or an email. That charity advert email was urgent but the request came when I was deep in the AppleInsider podcast, so having it just be found for me so quickly was such a boon.

I could've just searched my calendar, true. But then I asked Siri AI to find the concert tickets in one of my email accounts, and it did.

Similarly, there's a concert I was due to see last year but it was cancelled, then rescheduled, and when I suddenly worried that I'd missed the new date, it was Siri AI that said no, you're fine. You're seeing Dar Williams at this date and at this location, it told me, plus here's the email with the tickets.

On and on it goes, I'm practically at the stage of calling up Siri AI before I've finished thinking what I want. If I sound like an evangelist, it's because I now am and specifically so because macOS Golden Gate has made Siri AI so readily prominent and useful.

I would say that I no longer Google anything, I just ask Siri AI, but that's not entirely true. Siri AI doesn't always find what other AI services do, so I still keep Claude around.

Although while there presumably can't have been much work done by Apple on what it calls Siri's World Knowledge, I'm now only rarely finding Siri AI's answers to be wrong. For some reason that was different at the start of the beta test.

Siri AI always gives short answers to questions and usually they're too short.

However, for some unfathomable reason, Siri AI responses are still intentionally limited to how much you could say in a single breath. I'm sorry, but I have no particular concern over whether Siri runs out of breath or not.

So if I'm searching for something that I know will need more detail, then I will again turn to Claude.

Plus, let this be a public service announcement: Siri AI finally works with Apple Music. But only on the Mac.

Until the last moments of the macOS Golden Gate beta test, and still in the final iOS 27 beta, Siri AI would claim to be able to add Apple Music tracks to playlists. But it would then work only just often enough that you would keep trying.

Most of the time, the gigantic majority of the time, Siri AI would say it couldn't find the playlist you said. Even if just before, you had asked it to play that playlist and it had done so without complaint.

Apple Music and Siri AI integration was, and still is on iOS, enraging, partly because of how patronizing it could be. If you keep asking, Siri AI will eventually apologize for your confusion, as if it's you who is getting this wrong.

It was not chance that means Siri AI has been coded to say "I won't respond to that" when you tell it just precisely what you think of it.

I should be ecstatic that it's now working on the Mac, but on the one hand, I almost always use that particular feature on the iPhone while driving. And on the other, there was a whole twenty minutes during one beta release where it worked on the iPhone too.

You can't believe the surprise when Siri AI finally added an Apple Music track to a playlist, like it always said it could.

There weren't that many people using the beta, compared to how many will now have it. But Apple has the problem of convincing those beta users to try this feature again.

Which feels like an own goal because Apple already had the much greater issue of getting anyone to try Siri at all. Apple broke Siri two years ago and then left it like that.

Deep breath.

Nonetheless, you must try Siri AI on macOS Golden Gate and by itself, it is the reason to upgrade. You have to get on a waitlist, though.

What else macOS Golden Gate brings

Saying that Siri AI is the reason to upgrade is of course a way of stressing just how good it is, when it's good. But this is also close to strictly accurate as the only major update to macOS this time is Siri AI.

So there are refinements to Liquid Glass, for instance, but they're really just a sop to the vocal minority who don't like that redesign. Apple can tell you that there are now controls for adjusting just how liquid its Liquid Glass features are, for instance, and it's not lying.

There is a slider to adjust how liquid Apple's Liquid Glass design is, but it doesn't make much difference.

But you have to whack the slider fully to one way or the other to really distinguish any difference at all. Since I'm fine with Liquid Glass, I tried this, shrugged at it, and never went back.

Your mileage may vary, as alongside this overall Liquid Glass slider, there are improvements to individual elements. So you could fill your time trying out variations on the appearance of Dock icons, and that might be worth it.

I say that particularly because while I haven't done any of that appearance fiddling, Apple has. This is just me, I realise, but somehow through the betas I kept mistaking the Preview icon for the Keynote one.

L-R: The Keynote icon, the original Preview icon, and the final Preview one.

They're not even really that close, but something about them kept tripping me up. Then in the latest betas and now in the final release, Apple has changed the Preview icon and I no longer choose the wrong one.

Mind you, I prefer the previous Preview icon.

One other change during the beta process was that Apple removed the old toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence. I wondered at first whether that meant everyone was stuck with Apple Intelligence, but there is now a Turn Off Siri control which may do the same thing.

There's no toggle for turning off Apple Intelligence any more, but there is one for turning off the whole of Siri. Though you won't want to.

I wouldn't know, really, because originally I wasn't bothered by Apple Intelligence in any sense of the term. And now, specifically because of Siri AI, and specifically because of how it is on the Mac, Apple Intelligence is part of my daily workflow and I've no interest in turning it off.

Shortcuts

While Shortcuts works across the iPhone and iPad as well, I am most often creating them on the Mac. Which means my second favorite aspect of macOS Golden Gate is how Apple Intelligence has changed Shortcuts and made it much quicker to use.

Unfortunately, for several years, the Shortcuts action to open a Safari tab group has failed on the Mac. It works fine on the iPhone and the iPad where it's of little use, since you're already tapping on the screen.

The new Shortcuts app is very good at clearly saying what a Shortcut it creates will do. Except it sometimes doesn't do anything of the sort.

On the Mac, it would be so convenient to press a keystroke or tap a Stream Deck button to switch between Tab Groups. And you were supposed to be able to do exactly that.

You still can't, and some time in the last few beta test versions, Apple implemented a kind of solution. It removed the Open Tab Group action from the Mac.

It's unfathomable why Apple couldn't make this work when it added the action. But it's more unfathomable why the new Shortcuts will pretend to do it.

Seriously. It's a bad part of what is otherwise a brilliant feature, which is the Apple Intelligence version of Shortcuts.

Previously, Shortcuts would offer countless actions that you could drag into a list which it would then work through. You can still do this and you can still create complex Shortcuts by hand.

You can tell Shortcuts what you want in plain English and while far from flawless, it is remarkably good at creating just what you need.

But Apple has added Apple Intelligence to the simple plus button that gets you started. Once you click that, Shortcuts just asks you what you want to do, then it does the job of choosing the actions and assembling the Shortcut to do it.

There are times when this is so good that it is amazing and you think you'll never fashion a Shortcut manually again. For instance, there's a timing thing I need for the AppleInsider podcast and I could never quite work out the math, but Shortcuts did it immediately.

Yet there are times, such as with the Safari tab groups example, where Shortcuts will tell you that it has done what you asked. It will present a concise list of what precisely that Shortcut will do for you, even if it will not do anything of the sort.

It's not surprising that there are limits, of course. But it is surprising that there are these failures when sometimes Shortcuts will display an error message saying it can't do a particular thing.

So Apple Intelligence in Shortcuts is like Apple Intelligence in Siri AI. Absolutely fantastic, except when it's pants.

Shortcuts can build reasonably complex Shortcuts automatically.

Nonetheless, the ability to incredibly quickly make at least basic Shortcuts by just saying what you want, that's transformative. More Mac users will get into Shortcuts because of this.

And while I actually enjoy writing Shortcuts for myself, most of the time now I do start by asking for what I want. Of the last 20 Shortcuts I've made, all of them started this way, although 5 failed.

That's still a 75% success rate, which could well be better than my own.

Surprisingly useful Photo tools

Just as on iOS 27, macOS Golden Gate also includes Image Playground and it has been improved. I've not used it once for serious work, but I do see the improvement.

That's because for some reason, and who knows why, I once asked the previous version to create an image of five clowns carrying a horse. That version gave me too few clowns, too many horses, and looked dreadful.

That image is actually far better than the first betas of Image Playground could produce. But I asked for five clowns, not seven.

Trying the same prompt now, the image is vastly better and there is only one horse. But for some reason there are seven clowns. They seem happy.

What I have used for actual work is the way that Photos can now edit images. I was making a poster for my YouTube channel and needed more space for the text, so I had Photos extend my image.

It took moments. Open Photos, pop the image in, choose Edit, Tools, Extend, and then drag across where you want to widen the image. It didn't take Photos much longer to do the job.

And let this be proof of how well it did it. I did this a couple of months ago and staring at my YouTube channel, I cannot now remember or even guess which poster I did this with.

That was a real use-case for me, but I did experiment with the other photo manipulation features early on in the beta and originally had more limited results. So limited that I did not again try reframing a shot to move someone's eyeline, and I did not try to erase large sections of the image ever again.

Don't look at my silly hat, look at the Apple Store to the right. There was a whole person there before. And my own right arm is AI-generated.

Until just now. Trying it out again now, the results are staggeringly better than they were.

It must depend on the shot, but I had one of me and my wife in Vancouver, sitting against a glass partition in that city's great Apple Store. For obvious privacy reasons, I just now used Clean Up to remove my wife and I tell you, if we ever divorce, I'm going to use this instead of cutting up all our printed photos.

Clean Up removed her, and filled in the space not with some generic background, but what looks to me like what really was originally behind her. It has taken a sliver of an Apple Watch poster and recreated that, plus put some of those Apple Store wooden cube seats there.

But then I reframed it because for some reason I wasn't quite looking at the camera. It's like I thought I was a YouTube presenter or something.

There was only a slight reframing adjustment needed, but it did it. It did it with finer controls than there were and, most importantly for me, it did it so well that it truly looks like I was staring into the camera.

But to do that, I noticed that it filled in some more of the background around the edge of the frame. So I tried telling it to extend more and I chose the most difficult part.

In this shot, I am leaning into frame from the left, so I extended it out in that direction. And Photos made up my arm and jacket perfectly.

I'm still going to tell people to look into the lens, please. But what seemed like a toy at the start of the beta test is now a usable, potentially useful feature.

Writing Tools are a shrug, but a useful one

This bothers me because it's creating some material and I never imagined I'd do that. I'm certainly not going to be using macOS Golden Gate's Siri AI to write anything.

Although... It's now 31 years since Microsoft Word added red underlining for spell-checking and that means for three decades I've barely paid any attention to it. That's an exaggeration, but it's definitely true of the blue underlines you get when Word is bored and decides to make up grammar rules.

Yet during the beta test of macOS Golden Gate, I've been more conscious of Writing Tools. Never the actual feature, I don't think I've opened those more than once, but the gentle automatic underlining as I type has been rather good.

Once, Siri AI also went ahead and corrected the spelling in my document too.

Plus there was a time when, as I'm in England, I wasn't certain of the US spelling of a word. I called up Spotlight, asked Siri AI, and it told me I'd got it wrong, which was helpful.

Every time, too, I can type "Fix it" into Siri AI and it does, it amends my text. Once it just did that anyway: told me it was wrong, corrected it in my document and said "you're welcome."

Okay, it didn't say that, but it was still startling to see it happen. I don't understand why it did this that once, but even being able to ask it to fix the spelling of one specific word seems good to me.

Fantastic, staggering, and dreadful

You can tell I like macOS Golden Gate and you won't be remotely surprised to learn that I do not want to go back to macOS Tahoe. But it isn't all brilliant, and there are annoyances even beyond the peculiar problems with Shortcuts.

I say annoyances. Some are minor and actually I'm certain they are only because I'm writing this while still on one of the last betas. There's a bug right now about when you scrub through a video; the slider keeps snapping back to the start, for instance, and that will surely be fixed.

Or there is that great feature when you're saving a document and can click on the name of an existing one. That copies the existing name and you can just make some changes.

So I'll have video assets such as "Take 1" and can just replace that digit with 2 rather than typing out the whole name. That's been a thing on the Mac for as long as I can remember, but in the last betas it was working too quickly.

I would be in the Save dialog, move to a new folder, and find that my document title was immediately changed to that of something already there. It always seems to happen when I've taken the time to write a new document title, too, and that gets wiped out.

Similarly, a bug I've had that appears to still be here is that menus in Save dialogs won't always work. In Pixelmator Pro, for instance, I can't always specify that I want to export an image as PNG instead of JPEG because the menu flips back closed too quickly.

Of course the Phone app has separate audio controls from System Settings, although at least they are now under "Audio" instead of "Video."

But if there were one Mac thing I would wish Apple would fix... no, okay, one thing other than Shortcut tab group support, it is the Phone app.

This should be extraordinarily useful. To be able to make and receive calls on the Mac without getting out your iPhone, it should be so very handy.

But it does not work.

There has been one minor improvement. Originally it was that despite any other sound setting on your Mac, the Phone app had its own. It would sometimes even default to something you no longer had connected.

True, once you knew it did this ridiculous thing, you could change the audio setting. Once you also knew that to change anything to do with audio, though, you had to look under the Video menu.

This is now better. That same menu has been retitled Audio. Although while that lets me specify what microphone and speaker I want on one Mac, on another it won't. It just snaps back to whatever it was set to by default.

But it doesn't help even when you can set these. I have the correct microphone and speaker selected in it, but if I call someone, they cannot hear me.

I'd obviously like that to be fixed, please, and I struggle to understand why the problem hasn't been resolved yet. But then maybe I'm just a heavier phone user than most.

Only, since I am, I would also like to be able to answer or end calls with a keystroke or a Stream Deck button. As it is, I have to wait for the call notification to appear, then find the green answer button.

Even Keyboard Maestro clicks on that Answer Phone icon to no avail.

That notification is now appearing quicker than it did, so it's no longer the case that people have hung up before it's displayed. But clicking on that green answer button is a lottery because sometimes it just does not respond.

You could blame my hand/eye coordination, except for this. I went to the trouble of making a Keyboard Maestro macro and including in it a screenshot of that button.

Now I press a Stream Deck button, it launches that macro, Keyboard Maestro looks for the button, finds it, clicks it, and nothing happens.

I'd phone Apple to ask them about it, but...

Devils and details

The more you dig into anything, the more likely you are to find problems. I'm conscious that in the case of macOS Golden Gate, what are truly small irritations still manage to burrow under my skin.

I think you can rightly criticize me for that, it is surely a sign that I need to get out more. But perhaps it's also a sign of how important macOS is to me.

If you are a Mac user, it has always been astounding how much you can do with these devices. I've a relative who believes I am a computer geek because I'll spend 15 hours in front of my Mac, but to me that's not what I'm doing at all.

I'm writing articles, I'm editing video, I'm reading books, I am doing countless things that I need and enjoy and relish. A new macOS is just about the only thing that touches every part of that, every application, and every task.

So a new macOS is an enormous deal. And while I initially thought that Siri AI was the sole update in macOS Golden Gate, I do now see that there is more.

It's still the main update and it's still fantastic. But overall macOS Golden Gate is yet another example of how Apple makes you wonder why you put up with the previous version at all.

items.title: If you let it, Apple Intelligence will train itself on your data in iOS 27
items.summary: As it turns out, Apple realistically needs customer data to make Siri AI work well. So, starting with iOS 27, it is asking users to opt-in to training on your data.
items.content_html:
As it turns out, Apple realistically needs customer data to make Siri AI work well. So, starting with iOS 27, it is asking users to opt-in to training on your data.

A new section in the iOS 27 privacy policy shows that Apple has reversed its stance on using customers' data to train its AI models. Previously, the company assured customers that it had no need for customer data, and would figure out how to make Siri AI work well without it.

Apple maintains that it "takes steps to ensure that personal data is not stored or used by Apple." But as Heise points out, and Apple has said in the terms of service for a few years now, the audio material may be listened to by Apple employees after anonymization.

Currently, new feature is opt-in only. When iOS 27 rolls out on Monday, September 14, users will see a prompt that asks users to help improve the chatbot, with an agree or "not now" button.

It also admits that data collected may be reviewed by "review personnel." It is unclear if "review personnel" are Apple employees or a third-party company contracted to read conversation transcripts, as it has historically been.

The change is a big deal.

Apple has been trying to make Apple Intelligence less of the boogeyman that OpenAI's ChatGPT and Meta's MetaAI have become in the public eye.

Of course, Apple has been training its AI on user data for a while now. It just came up with a complex, yet controversial method to do so, dubbed Differential Privacy.

That method required Apple to provide artificial prompts it believes are popular and then look for pattern matches in user data analytics. Then, because of artificially injected noise and a threshold of needing hundreds of fragment matches, there wouldn't be any way to surface unique or individual-identifying prompts.

But when it comes to Siri AI queries, the company likely needs to actually hear how users are interfacing with the assistant. At least if it wants to remain competitive.

The timing is notable, as Apple's newest Apple Watch models are designed to continuously listen for conversations. Users can request a transcript of the previous 15 seconds at any time, with the audio purged after the transcript is generated.

Siri Recap can also provide users with summaries of conversations from throughout the day. Apple says the feature relies on Private Cloud Compute.

That raises questions about what data could eventually become eligible for Apple's AI training program. As of yet, Apple hasn't said Apple Watch conversation data will be included.

It was inevitable

Apple was always going to get to this point. It was never a matter of if, but rather a matter of when.

Apple has been behind in the artificial intelligence race for quite some time now. And to keep pace with the rest of its competitors, whether it's Meta or OpenAI or Anthropic, it needs to analyze what works and what doesn't work with Siri.

And, unfortunately, to do so, it's going to have to access data. If you allow it, your data, specifically.

Apple's betting that some users will opt in. However, with more and more people growing skeptical of AI, that may not be the safest bet.

I personally doubt that, at least in the medium-term, Apple will force every user to submit to The Data Harvest. I do suspect, though, that the company may force that option in the future if you wish to use Apple Intelligence.

The real question is whether or not Apple will allow Apple Intelligence to remain opt-in forever. And I grow increasingly concerned that, eventually, the company will stop giving users that choice.

Update September 14, 11:56 AM ET: Removed how to opt out, pending final iOS 27 release.

items.title: Apple has 16 products in line for future release
items.summary: Apple just revealed the iPhone Duo, but that doesn't mean the company is anywhere close to finished for the year. Here are the 16 upcoming products rumored to be coming before the end of 2026 and into 2027.
items.content_html:
Apple just revealed the iPhone Duo, but that doesn't mean the company is anywhere close to finished for the year. Here are the 16 upcoming products rumored to be coming before the end of 2026 and into 2027.

The release cycle never ends for a multi-trillion dollar company, and Apple fans are well aware of that. Every product is on a release cycle, so many are easy to predict down to the month or day of release.

According to a new rumor roundup, at least 16 of Apple's upcoming products are known. If you've been following AppleInsider's reporting, none of these should come as any surprise.

The remainder of 2026 includes these seven products:

  • HomePod mini with Siri AI
  • Apple TV with Siri AI
  • Apple Home Hub tablet
  • Touch Screen MacBook Pro
  • 14-inch MacBook Pro with M6
  • iMac with M6
  • iPad mini with OLED

The first half of 2027 should reveal the following nine products:

  • MacBook Air with M6
  • MacBook Neo with A19 Pro
  • iPad with Siri AI
  • iPad Pro with M6
  • iPad Air with M5 and OLED
  • iPhone 18
  • iPhone 18e
  • iPhone Air 2
  • Apple Pencil Pro and Apple Pencil with USB-C upgrades

Those keeping up with Apple's release cycles shouldn't be surprised by most of this list. The iPad Pro with M5 update fits Apple's usual 18-month or so cycle, and new Apple Pencil models make sense given the launch of iPhone Duo.

New MacBook models, the long-rumored base iPad upgrade, and the base iPhone models are all within expectation for Apple's release cycle as well. Rumors indicated Apple could have released an updated base iPad at any time, but likely waited for Siri AI to finalize the product, like with Apple TV, HomePod mini, and Home Hub.

Catch up on the latest rumors with AppleInsider's coverage and rumor roundups here:

  • Apple's Home Hub tablet rumors
  • iPhone Air 2 due in the spring
  • OLED and touchscreen MacBook Pro models
  • iPad mini with OLED

The origin of this list comes from a Bloomberg report. AppleInsider has rated this as likely as it aligns with release cycles and tons of previous rumors.

items.title: New Apple TV with Siri AI could launch at any time in the fall
items.summary: Apple reportedly held back on releasing new Apple TV hardware until its Apple Intelligence upgrades were ready, so expect the upgraded set-top box at any time.
items.content_html:
Apple reportedly held back on releasing new Apple TV hardware until its Apple Intelligence upgrades were ready, so expect the upgraded set-top box at any time.

The slow rollout of Apple Intelligence in 2024 followed by a delay and rethink has caused several pieces of hardware to get shelved. The long-rumored Home Hub tablet, the next-generation Apple TV, and the other Apple Home products all need the new Siri AI to get the most out of them.

According to the "Power On" newsletter from Bloomberg, Monday's launch of Siri AI with iOS 27 is finally what will allow these dormant products to release. Specifically, it calls out the updated Apple TV as due sometime this fall.

While Apple TV has never been Apple's most powerful product, it tends to get a modern chipset to run whatever version of tvOS is available at the time. The current model, which was released in 2022, runs the A15 processor.

Apple TV with Siri AI

Rumors suggest Apple will include the A19 or A19 Pro with the upcoming Apple TV. While that's not quite state-of-the-art since the A20 now exists, it is likely more than enough for the Apple TV.

That new chipset should come with more RAM, up to 12GB. Not only will that be useful for onboard AI processing, but gaming.

Yes, the Apple TV is often forgotten for being capable of running games at all, but the A19 chipset family is no slouch with its graphics capabilities. Slapping that chipset in a device with continuous AC power and active cooling could prove interesting.

However, the primary use case and pitch of the new Apple TV will be artificial intelligence. Siri AI will be much more capable on the device, plus HomeKit Secure Video camera recordings can be processed with AI analysis locally.

Given how many Apple Home products are expected later in 2026, there may be a special event held to announce them. Although, Apple has been known to shove things out via press release alongside short video productions for each product.

Whatever Apple decides to do, expect an updated Apple TV no later than November. The recent price hike to $199 and $249 should stick for the new hardware, which should also include a new Siri Remote.

attachments.title: New Apple TV with Siri AI could launch at any time in the fall

items.title: It's not clear why Elon Musk has filed to dismiss App Store favoritism suit

items.content_html:
Elon Musk has moved to dismiss its lawsuit against Apple regarding the App Store given preferential treatment to OpenAI over xAI's apps. There are unanswered questions.

The court filing on Monday, September 14 is pretty sparse, other than the request to dismiss. It's not yet clear if there's some kind of settlement, or if Musk has decided his case is baseless.

OpenAI was named in the suit as well. Notably, it's just Apple that Musk is asking the court to remove from the case, and OpenAI will need to fight two major legal battles with industry titans at the same time.

Apple and OpenAI were sued by Elon Musk's xAI, now owned by SpaceX, due to alleged anticompetitive practices. The trial hasn't been going well for Musk so far, as it was accused of destroying and withholding evidence previously.

The suit alleging preferential treatment has been sketchy from the beginning. As Musk's own Grok noted when asked by a social media user, other companies other than OpenAI have been on the top of the App Store.

DeepSeek was in the App Store top spot in January 2025. Perplexity followed on July 18, 2025. Both happened after the June 2024 OpenAI and Apple partnership.

Further complicating the suit, app data aggregator SensorTower has also noted that Grok was on the peak App Store spot on February 18, 2025 and February 19, 2025 after Grok-3 was made free.

The case has been moving at a snail's pace since it was brought on August 2025. In May 2026, SVP of Software Engineering Craig Federighi was brought in as a document custodian.

Current Apple CEO Tim Cook was also requested as a custodian, but that was denied.

And, more recently, a judge has ruled that Elon Musk's emails must be entered into the record. It's still not clear what has triggered Musk's request.

We have reached out to Apple and X corp for more details. We are not expecting a response from either, but a return call from Apple is more likely.

items.title: iPhone 18 Pro pre-orders off to a surprisingly slow start
items.summary: Whether it's because of the economy, better supply than normal, the looming iPhone Duo, or Apple's unusual opening of pre-orders on a Saturday, very few iPhone 18 Pro models are showing any shipping delays as of an hour after preorder start.
items.content_html:
Whether it's because of the economy, better supply than normal, the looming iPhone Duo, or Apple's unusual opening of pre-orders on a Saturday, very few iPhone 18 Pro models are showing any shipping delays as of an hour after preorder start.

Following their launch on September 9, 2026, the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max models are now available for pre-order. But they did not sell out immediately, as is more normally the case.

By 08:30 ET, half an hour after pre-orders opened, no color or configuration of the iPhone 18 Pro showed any shipping delays at all in the US. They remained available to be delivered on Friday, September 18.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max fared better, but not by much. None of the 1TB or 2TB versions are delayed whatsoever.

But the first model to see any delay was the iPhone 18 Pro Max 256GB one in burgundy. Shortly after 30 minutes, it slipped from September 18 to between September 29 and October 6, which is around a week and a half to two weeks later.

By the one-hour mark, that model was delayed a further week, showing as October 6 to October 13. The 512 burgundy model initially slipped to between September 24 and September 29, but by 09:00 ET it too was October 6 to October 13.

Similarly, the glacier color iPhone 18 Pro Max 256GB slipped to up to two weeks after half an hour, and so did the same configuration in silver. It's now showing October 6 to October 13, and the black 512GB model is September 24 to September 29, while it's still September 18 in silver.

The black iPhone 18 Pro Max 256GB model also slipped to September 24 as its earliest delivery date.

These are all figures for the US Apple Store and there has been a difference overseas. In the UK, for instance, all but the 2TB version of the burgundy iPhone 18 Pro slipped back to September 24.

What's happening

Moving to Saturday to open pre-orders, in order to not be on 9/11, has surely had an impact as people's schedules and availability will be different. There is also the fact that it's not yet possible to pre-order the iPhone Dou, so buyers may be waiting for that model.

Or there is the fact that the global chip shortage has made prices higher. Plus the global economy is such that discretionary spending is reduced.

However, it is also possible that Apple has done a better job of predicting early sales demand and managed to produce sufficient quantities to meet it.

items.title: Craig Federighi admits iPhone Duo may replace iPads for some users
items.summary: Apple usually does a careful job of separating its products so that they each have distinct use cases, but Craig Federighi has now acknowledged that the iPhone Duo does overlap with the iPad mini.
items.content_html:
Apple usually does a careful job of separating its products so that they each have distinct use cases, but Craig Federighi has now acknowledged that the iPhone Duo does overlap with the iPad mini.

Apple's iPhone Duo, and especially its price tag, immediately raised the issue that users could get the same benefits by buying a regular iPhone and an iPad mini. Now Apple's senior vice president of software engineering, Craig Federighi, has talked about overlapping devices.

"I agree for someone who maybe had an iPad mini... this device can often fill that space for them," he told Marques Brownlee in a short YouTube interview.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

Federighi stopped short of saying there was no longer any reason to buy an iPad, though. He said that this was another case where Apple's devices find their use cases.

"I think we had the same question when people said, hey, well, I have an iPad and a Mac, like, when are you going to use one or the other?" said Federighi. "And I think we all fall into very natural patterns in our lives or the kinds of activities where we just naturally feel like, okay, the Mac's the right tool for the job, the iPad's the right tool for the job."

"I think very naturally, it's going to play out that way with this device," he continued. "So, I think people are gonna find their way."

Federighi revealed that he's been using an iPhone Duo for months and it has indeed found a place for him. "If I am starting on the iPhone... and I actually just want to go deeper into a piece of content," he explained, "this device is extraordinary to open up, often open in portrait, actually, and page through some content."

Public response

Federighi was also asked about the public reaction to the device and he had a similar response to senior vice president of worldwide marketing, Greg Joswiak's.

Joswiak was delighted at how much Apple had managed keep secret. Federighi says he liked how people were surprised by what Apple had done with the device.

"This was exciting in that I think people didn't fully anticipate how much we were going to adapt the software experience to the form factor," he said. I hope, as people do spend time with it, that's what they take home is not hardware, our software apart, but how we brought them together."

Considering that the iPhone Duo has been rumored for years, both men are right about how surprisingly good it still managed to be.

A leaker with a reasonable track record has sketchy details of what they claim Samsung's iPhone Duo display deal is with Apple.

It was already known that Samsung makes the displays for the iPhone Duo, and also that the screen company had an exclusive deal. Apple was seemingly forced to accept the arrangement because no other firm was able to supply the required screens.

Now according to leaker Instant Digital posting on the Chinese social media site Weibo, the deal is a three-year one. It's to cover the current iPhone Duo and future models during that time, and they say Samsung is charging $250 per panel.

Previous reports say that Apple's other main display manufacturer, LG Display, does not yet make folding screens. BOE makes them for Huawei, but reportedly Apple considers those inadequate, plus it regularly has problems with that company's reliability.

While overall component prices are known to have risen for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, previously Apple was offering Samsung and LG Display around $70 per display panel.

The interior screen on the iPhone Duo is of course vastly more complex than the one on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, so it's unsurprising that it would cost considerably more to manufacture. But it means that the display is an unusually high proportion of the costs of manufacturing, representing around an eighth of the iPhone Duo's retail price.

That $250 price does not include any costs of assembly or testing. It also presumably only applies to the interior screen, as the leaker does not mention the exterior or front screen.

Instant Digital has a reasonable reputation for accuracy. They may well be one of the people Apple's Greg Joswiak was thinking of when he said that it was unfortunate that some leakers had got details of the iPhone Duo.

items.title: macOS Tahoe 26.4 update stops you from copying your login Keychain
items.summary: Apple's changes to the Keychain in macOS Tahoe made it more secure. However, by binding it to device-specific Secure Enclave keys, users now can't manually copy the login Keychain and use it on another Mac.
items.content_html:
Apple's changes to the Keychain in macOS Tahoe made it more secure. However, by binding it to device-specific Secure Enclave keys, users now can't manually copy the login Keychain and use it on another Mac.

Attacks on Mac users are getting more sophisticated over time, with AI also opening the door to even more malware and the discovery of new intrusion techniques. While Apple does work to increase the security of its operating systems and software to counter the threats, they can also become a burden to administrators.

In a blog post on September 8, Rich Trouton wrote that it wasn't possible to manually copy login Keychain files from one Mac to another. At least, doing so and still being able to use them on the new machine.

As he explains, the login keychain is a SQLite database file stored in the user's home folder, which you could previously copy from one Mac to a second. While you could use the file straight away on earlier versions, an update to macOS Tahoe meant that it wouldn't work for Macs using a Secure Enclave.

The Secure Enclave guards the metadata key that protects the keychain attributes required to decrypt it. The change means that the Secure Enclave must be used whenever the login Keychain file is accessed.

The metadata key can be cached in the Application Processor for fast keychain entries. However, the Secure Enclave must be accessed for that cache to exist in the first place.

If you've moved the Keychain file to another Mac, it won't have access to the Secure Enclave, and therefore won't open.

Changed chain in macOS Tahoe

While the change is only really becoming known now, it's something that actually happened back in March. According to Trouton and another September 10 post by Jeff Johnson, the macOS 26.4 update introduced it.

Testing confirmed that the ability to copy the file worked for macOS 26.3, including via a virtual machine. However, copying the login Keychain from a virtual machine running macOS 26.4 didn't work, due to not being able to be read on other Macs.

Other non-login Keychain files are unaffected and can be unlocked on other Macs fine.

In an addendum on September 11, Johnson writes that this was a "ticking time bomb" that Apple included in a minor macOS update. For macOS 26.3 and earlier, Johnson explains that users could recover their login Keychain on a new Mac, but that's not possible on macOS 26.4 by copying it over.

In an emergency and with the death of a Mac, Johnson says users would only discover the login Keychain wouldn't work at the worst possible moment. "This is incredibly irresponsible of Apple," he concludes.

Exceptions and workarounds

It is evident that a straight copy of the login Keychain and opening it elsewhere simply won't work. The hardened security is there to stop malicious actors from doing just that.

However, it is only a problem if you are copying your credentials in this particular way.

For users who are restoring backups to the same Mac, they will not be affected by the issue, as it's the same Mac. It also won't affect anyone using Migration Assistant, though it will be a problem for administrators performing bulk migrations in a corporate environment.

Exporting items before a migration is also a way around the issue, as well as the use of custom keychains and other password managers.

For home users, taking advantage of iCloud Keychain may be the route ahead. As well as ensuring your passwords are shared to your iPhone and iPad, they can also be synchronized with your other Macs.

items.title: Apple Intelligence could be the key to cram Face ID into future iPhone Duo

items.content_html:
A new report obviously predicts that Apple wants to replace the iPhone Duo's existing Touch ID with Face ID as soon as possible, and suggests that Apple Intelligence might help.

Touch ID is easily the most apparent compromise in the iPhone Duo, and Apple has had to go back it because of that model's slim chassis. It was not physically possible to fit the usual Face ID components into that space.

Now Bloomberg has made the obvious prediction that Apple will be working to add Face ID to future generations of the iPhone Duo. But it's also suggested that AI could be part of the solution.

The claim is that Apple Intelligence could ultimately help with not just the iPhone's computational photography, but also all of its image processing. So Apple could in theory use less sophisticated depth-sensing camera systems and let AI take up more of the processing role.

That would then presumably mean that the physical Face ID components could be smaller. The prediction is that this will not happen until the third generation of the iPhone Duo, by which time the report also expects the model to gain a telephoto camera.

This is also an obvious prediction and the third generation iPhone Duo is sufficiently far off to make it an easy guess. But the suggestion of AI augmenting the hardware components would fit Apple's unusual ability of entirely controlling its software and hardware together.

items.title: Apple Store Genius Bar & pickup counter revamp effort accelerating
items.summary: Apple's slow-walk of store refurbishment to the new "standard" is getting a boost, with Genius Bar, pickup table, and Avenue updates on the way to more stores, faster.
items.content_html:
Apple's slow-walk of store refurbishment to the new "standard" is getting a boost, with Genius Bar, pickup table, and Avenue updates on the way to more stores, faster.

Apple retail sales efforts focus on Apple Stores as more than just a place to buy hardware, but also a local and physical representation of the brand. As the company's leadership changes, so too is the company's retail strategy.

According Mark Gurman in Sunday's "Power On" newsletter for Bloomberg, there will be a big shake-up on the way for Apple's retail arm.

For a start, instead of continuing a rapid expansion and bringing stores to new places quickly, it will instead be more selective on where it will open them. Rather than widening the reach, Apple is picking up the pace on store renovations around the world in the coming years.

Eclectic Avenues

The revamp will focus on three areas of the Apple Store itself. A big one is the update to the Avenue, referring to the sections on the sides of the stores for accessories and Apple Services.

There will be two new Avenue sections, including one for online pick-ups and another for Today at Apple hands-on sessions. While the current store layout use a dedicated pick-up table and a large seating area, they will be put into their own 10-foot bays.

The online pick-up bay will be made completely from wood, with the upper half featuring an Apple logo while the lower will have secured drawers for orders. A table will be in front for employees to actually conduct the handoff to customers.

Today at Apple's Avenue bay will also be wood, with the top section looking like an oversized TV. The lower section will again use secured drawers to hold equipment.

In front will be a fixed table for the instructor as well as a few surrounding stools.

Genius Bars and bye-bye video walls

A second change will be the removal of the large video walls at many stores. While used for Today at Apple sessions and for marketing videos, Apple will be removing them so that it can have more space for more traditional retail elements.

For most stores, this will be replaced by new Genius Bars, again all-wood in construction. Two counter heights will be used for accessibility, with a background of storage drawers and large product posters.

The Genius Bar at the Tysons Corner Apple Store in 2023.

AppleInsider was at the reopening of the Tysons Corner store, which is an exemplar of that strategy. Our photo from that 2023 refurbishment shows what the company has in mind for the Genius Bar, as a fairly long wooden line along one wall.

The new bars and other changes will be made to integrate with existing store designs, so they look like they were always meant to be part of the original design.

Changes will also affect staff-facing areas, including new break rooms and updated back-of-house areas. Staff will also face stricter morning meeting rules, including not drinking or using devices and staying standing throughout.

All store employees will also be expected to applaud the first customers to enter the store each day.

Testing and rollout

Gurman writes that some of these changes have already been used in some Apple Stores, as we've demonstrated. The plan now is to roll out this design chain-wide, and faster than originally planned.

This has apparently involved testing concepts internationally. A more global rollout will also take place over the next few years.

Before Apple's event, there were rumors of Apple preparing a store refresh. However, that was intended to be a way to promote Apple's smart home devices, which were not announced during the September presentation.

These changes could certainly arrive in the future alongside new products.

items.title: Why your iPhone Duo will inevitably develop a screen crease
items.summary: The iPhone Duo developing a crease over time is inevitable as the tides, and a matter of physics and engineering. Here's how and why that crease develops, and what Apple has done to mitigate it.
items.content_html:
The iPhone Duo developing a crease over time is inevitable as the tides, and a matter of physics and engineering. Here's how and why that crease develops, and what Apple has done to mitigate it.

In the run-up to Apple's folding iPhone, there was a lot of chatter about how Apple has "solved the smartphone crease." It's always been a silly topic, as there is no solving it, there is only postponing it.

It's an engineering problem on top of a physics problem. The physics are immutable.

What can be controlled is engineering tolerances, coupled with precise engineering, tailored to known stress points. It's about working around the issues of a hybrid screen, with the properties of both glass and plastic.

Plastic OLED and very, very thin glass layers

On its own, the OLED screen substrate is not rigid, and can bend and flex because it is essentially plastic. It too can break and tear, and is very soft, Because it is soft, it lacks what makes glass a good material for a smartphone touch surface.

Any type of glass, including Gorilla Glass, is a non-crystalline, amorphous solid. It's generally characterized by high chemical resistance, and a hardness which makes it a good smartphone touch surface, where the screen isn't.

Glass has poor thermal conductivity. And, it has a low coefficient of thermal expansion which makes it good for a smartphone screen.

Importantly, especially here, it is somewhat elastic. Especially when very thin.

To that end, folding smartphone glass is not one sheet. Ultra-thin glass, which is both a product name and a descriptor, is sandwiched in layers. Each layer is thinner than a human hair.

Each layer has with a coat of sliding adhesive. When the device is open and closed, this allows the layers to remain intact and slide very slightly across its neighbor. A thicker, single piece of glass would crack and shatter, versus the bend and slide

The hinge makes sure every fold is about the same, and optimized for minimal and even stretching of the glass.

This hinge means everything to the iPhone Duo screen

Extremely thin glass isn't new. Apple's glass partner Corning made Willow Glass in 2012, and has been selling it on rolls ever since.

At the time, it was used for static curved screens, long before the first folding smartphone, and basically at the dawn of the OLED era. The two combined has led to where we are now.

And, it will crease. Every folding screen will, even Apple's.

Fatigue failure and that crease

For years, there has been discussion of that crease in smartphones. It was very apparent on early smartphones with plastic screens because of the material properties of plastic.

Arguably, most failures will be from user drops and other impacts. That's not what we're talking about here, but a drop will aggravate a crease formation.

Progressive fatigue on that hinge point is the main factor behind obvious crease development.

Crush a can in the center, and bend it until it tears. That is a practical, accelerated demonstration of the same way that a crease in a smartphone develops over time.

Apple is not immune to remorseless physics. Engineering can mitigate physics somewhat, though. The hinge is a key factor.

I'm reasonably confident that Apple has engineered a hinge that will retain its tightness and regularity. The uniform and precise fold, each and every time, will limit the variables that need to be controlled to minimize fatigue damage, because the folds are uniform and the stress points are known.

Every material has a minimum bend radius where the material will fail, or take damage. I spoke about this briefly above, but the hinge keeps the glass on the correct side of that line with an arc, not strictly a bend.

But, still, over time, micro-cracks will emerge along the hinge point. And over time, the screen will start to delaminate just a bit.

All of this damage is accumulative. Fortunately, most screens, likely including Apple's, are rated to survive about 250,000 folds over a product's lifetime.

Some napkin math suggests that's more than 125 shut-to-open and back again cycles per day over five years.

Along the way, though, that accumulating damage will be visually and touch-evident at the point of maximum stress. That point is the center of the hinge.

That point is the crease. A crease, even on Apple's $2000 folding iPhone, is inevitable. It is a matter of time, and use.

Apple and engineering

Every single engineering problem is a compromise between physics, the material that can be used, the engineering you can bring to bear, and the cost it extracts to make the material. It's been long said that Apple over-engineers a problem.

I can't think of a problem that needs an "over-engineered" solution more than minimizing accumulated fatigue in a hinged material.

Apple has had seven years to look at competitors and see how their engineering has failed, and how it's been engineered around. That's a lot of flaming data to use, and make sure that your product doesn't crash and burn like that.

Apple has done well here, but how well it has done is up to time and contact with consumers. There are already concerns about the folding, and there are going to be the idiots in Apple stores who like to pound on demo hardware, which will accelerate those cycles.

Expect to see people opening and closing the iPhone Duo dozens of times in minutes, grinning like a fool when they do it and recording it on their own iPhones for social media cred. This isn't FineWoven where the problems were obvious, so don't rely on those videos for any measure of success or failure.

We're also sure that Apple will capture every single one of those units that gets pounded on at retail and test it to the point of total destruction, like they do.

Phones will be destroyed for YouTube clicks, and the folks with infant failures that do happen, will complain disproportionately loud on social media.

Enjoy your tech. Being concerned about the crease at this juncture is a waste of your time, like min-maxing your battery with operational habits that may or may not help is now.

While the crease is inevitable, there is no indication today that it is a show-stopper. The phones are designed to be used, they are designed to be open and shut, they are designed to get that Uber, to watch that video, to surf that site.

We still have hooks inside Apple Stores' service departments. Let us watch the numbers, let us figure out if it's a giant problem like the stage lights on the 13-inch MacBook Pro a few years ago, or the butterfly keyboard was. Let us figure out if it's a problem that deserves some non-hysterical watching and discussion like the orange iPhone turning pink for some folks with an coating misapplication at the factory in some early production units.

And, Apple replaced or fixed all of those actual issues.

Until then, ignore the folks that test to failure, and use your iPhone Duo. Report issues to Apple, and we'll let you know if there's a problem over time.

attachments.title: iPhone Duo will have a screen crease over time

items.title: Apple Lakeside gets a major redesign after nearly 20 years
items.summary: Apple Lakeside will reopen on September 12 following a redesign that adds dedicated pickup, expanded accessibility features, and a brand new experience room.
items.content_html:
Apple Lakeside will reopen on September 12 following a redesign that adds dedicated pickup, expanded accessibility features, and a brand new experience room.

Located in Essex, England, Apple Lakeside was initially opened in October 2007. The renovation has brought several upgrades to the space.

A new dedicated "Apple Pickup" area allows customers to order online and pick up when it is most convenient for them. It also boasts a sustainable choice of materials.

Accessibility was a key part of the redesign. Apple has included variable-height seating and tables, assisted listening systems, and enhanced visual and acoustic clarity; wheelchair users can take advantage of easier-to-navigate routes, too.

"We're excited to open the completely redesigned and upgraded Apple Lakeside, offering customers from across Essex and South East England new ways to discover and shop the latest Apple lineups," an Apple spokesperson said.

"The all-new Apple Lakeside features an experience room for customers to explore products, a designated Genius Bar to get personalised support, a dedicated Apple Pick Up area to conveniently collect online orders, and free, educational Today at Apple sessions that inspire customers to go further with their passions."

Like other Apple retail spaces, it runs on 100% renewable energy.

Apple lists Apple Lakeside as open through September 10, before a one-day closure on September 11. The redesigned store will open at 9:00 a.m. local time on September 12.

The upgrade comes as part of Apple's larger effort to modernize its stores worldwide. In 2023, it was reported that Apple would open or renovate 50 stores worldwide by 2027.

Apple opened its first UK store on Regent Street in 2004. The company currently has 39 stores in the UK.

Apple is set to permanently close the Apple Festival Place, located in Basingstoke, England, in November 2026.

Apple's latest flagship iPhones are up for grabs, with launch-day delivery dates set to slip quickly as orders pile up.

The Apple Store is back online, with preorders for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max now officially open. This time around, Apple has a queue system, versus refresh-hammering, and will open the order page when it has reached your spot in the queue.

Apple offered a preorder preparation option ahead of the launch, allowing buyers to select their preferred configuration and payment method. Those selections can speed up checkout now that preorders are live.

Apple scheduled iPhone 18 Pro preorders to begin at 5:00 a.m. Pacific, or 8:00 a.m. Eastern. Store access can still vary as Apple's website and Apple Store app come back online.

Some buyers may see the store before others, depending on how they access it and their location. AppleInsider can confirm that iPhone 18 Pro preorders are now live, with the aforementioned queue.

Buyers can also try switching between the website and Apple Store app.

Delivery dates for the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max will begin slipping as preorder demand builds. Popular colors, storage capacities, and configurations can move beyond launch-day delivery quickly.

The iPhone 18 Pro lineup starts at $1,199. The standard iPhone 18 is not part of this launch and will likely be announced in early 2027.

Apple's iPhone 18 Pro is powered by a vapor-cooled A20 Pro chip and has a 48MP Fusion Main camera.

items.title: Sunday Reboot: Apple Event's static structure and Ternus exists
items.summary: In this week's Sunday Reboot, the Apple Event rolled on as expected, but while it was his first big show as CEO, John Ternus had a muted introduction.
items.content_html:
In this week's Sunday Reboot, the Apple Event rolled on as expected, but while it was his first big show as CEO, John Ternus had a muted introduction.

Sunday Reboot is a weekly column covering some of the lighter stories within the Apple reality distortion field from the past seven days. All to get next week underway with a good first step.

Apple Event is Apple Event

Being in a role for a long period of time means you get to see patterns. For someone working the Apple beat, they'll experience that all the time.

In my case, the pattern wasn't just that there would be an event in September to introduce new iPhones. That's so ingrained into society that even newborn babies know that now.

I'm talking about the flow of the event itself. The format of the presentation, what happens on which beat, and so on.

The usual schedule for an event is:

  1. Entertaining introduction before CEO appears.
  2. CEO welcomes the viewers and passes initial comments before hinting at the first thing to launch.
  3. Flashy camera sequence passing to another executive to handle the actual product launch.
  4. Another sequence to pass to an underling about a specific feature of a product then back to the previous executive. Repeat as necessary.
  5. Executive either repeats with a second product from the same family or wraps up launch details, potentially leaving some for CEO to utter. Hands back to CEO.
  6. Repeat from 3 for X number of products.
  7. Depending on the rumors, a 1-in-3 chance of a final major product launch, possibly framed as "One more thing," complete with transition sequence to managing executive to present. Similar treatment of features before final hand-back to CEO
  8. CEO sums up the last item, covers all products, thanks viewers for watching.
  9. Presentation ends with another final sequence, Apple logo, and YouTube suggesting you watch one of the Underdogs ads.

A lot has already been written about the products Apple has shown during the event, but it's worth pointing out that the structure of the overall presentation didn't change one bit.

Even with a new CEO in the form of John Ternus, there wasn't any real thing that jumped out as an obvious alteration.

For Apple, this was ideal. It shows that, even with a new pair of hands at the wheel, the company is plodding on as usual.

That said, there is one bit about the event that doesn't seem to quite fit: the run time.

At 1 hour and 17 minutes, it was a brisk presentation to show off two smartphone models (three if you include the iPhone 18 Pro Max), the AirPods 5, and the new Apple Watch lineup.

That's not a long time at all, really. And yet Apple managed to pack a lot of stuff in there.

But at the same time, it felt a little empty. The rumors said there were massive smart home changes on the way, and maybe even an OLED iPad mini.

We didn't get that, but we did get the signs that the company is still stable, via the medium of prepared product launches and flashy editing.

John who?

As the first major event after becoming CEO you would think the presentation would be very heavy-handed about it. Ternus, a relative unknown to the general public, was to have his first prominent appearance as the face of the iPhone maker.

Thankfully, Apple didn't go down that route. Though to be fair, Ternus didn't need that anyway.

The only thing Ternus really needed was provided by a brief appearance by the guy he replaced. Tim Cook, famous for "Good morning," was brought onboard for a few seconds so viewers could be assured it definitely was an Apple Event, before handing over to the next chief.

Old CEO Tim Cook saying to look at the distant and blurry visage of the new CEO, John Ternus - Image Credit: Apple

Quite frankly, this was needed, because my mother knows who Tim Cook is, and that he's no longer CEO. She has no idea who John Ternus is, and after the event, still isn't entirely sure.

I'd bet that some members of the public watching it will also wonder who this new face is. Cook's fame at least helps Ternus make a splash in people's minds.

I say "make a splash." It's more "tried not to rock the boat."

For being the brand new CEO at a major company, it's weird that the event doesn't actually go out of its way to mention the guy's name.

His introduction talks about spending a lot of his life at Apple, and how it is an "extraordinary privilege" it is to show what the teams at Apple have come up with this year. It's very much a team effort, with Ternus almost taking the role of a generic host figure.

Sure, it's good for the company morale if his first words are all about the people working at the company. But while he's the frontman, he's practically anonymous to the public.

Subscribe to AppleInsider on YouTube

A check of the transcript reveals that "John" is said four times (and "Johny" once) and "Ternus" isn't mentioned at all. It's not brought up in the video notes on YouTube, seen by almost 50 million people by Sunday.

It would've cost a few seconds to say something like "Hi, I'm John, the new CEO at Apple," before going into the "doing it for the teams" talk. Or even Cook uttering "John" once would have done the trick.

After a few events, there will have been time for Ternus to make a bigger impact on the world. He will be a more well-known figure through interviews and other appearances in the coming years.

Eventually, he will get the public fame Tim Cook achieved. At some point, my mother will look at him and actually know his first name and that he's "that guy who does the iPhones."

But, for the moment, he will be known by some as "that guy who replaced Tim Cook." Hopefully that will change sooner rather than later.

Last week's Sunday Reboot discussed the transition from Cook to Ternus.
